nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Ruritanian romance and the adventure novel
literary_identity: Novelist and playwright; the author of The Prisoner of Zenda and the inventor of the Ruritanian romance.
biography: Born Anthony Hope Hawkins in London on 9 February 1863, the son of a school headmaster; he was educated at Marlborough and Balliol College, Oxford, and practised as a barrister until the success of The Prisoner of Zenda (1894) allowed him to write full time. He wrote over thirty novels, served as a war correspondent in the First World War, and was knighted in 1918. He died at Walton-on-the-Hill, Surrey, on 8 July 1933.
literary_profile: Hope invented the Ruritanian romance: The Prisoner of Zenda created a fictional central Europe of small kingdoms, court intrigue and swordfights, and in doing so created a formula that has never left the popular imagination. He was also a considerable writer of the English social novel, and his best work — The Dolly Dialogues, Rupert of Hentzau — shows a light, ironic talent that the Zenda industry has obscured.
stylistic_characteristics: Fast-moving adventure narrative with a first-person narrator; the fictional kingdom with its invented geography and protocol; the double and the impostor; swordplay and the set-piece escape; ironic comedy of manners in the social novels; the light, assured dialogue.
intellectual_concerns: Royalty, legitimacy and the impostor; courage, loyalty and the gentleman's code; court intrigue and the small kingdom; love and renunciation; the Englishman abroad; honour and the duel.
historical_significance: Hope created the Ruritanian romance, one of the most durable formulas in popular fiction: The Prisoner of Zenda has never been out of print, it gave the language the word 'Ruritanian', and it stands at the head of a tradition that runs through Graustark to The Prisoner of Zenda's many film versions.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the comic short story and the tale of terror
literary_identity: Short-story writer and dramatist; the author of 'The Monkey's Paw' and the finest English comic writer of the sea and the riverside.
biography: Born William Wymark Jacobs in Wapping, London, on 8 September 1863, the son of a wharf manager; he worked as a clerk in the savings-bank department of the Post Office while writing stories of the London docks, and his first collection, Many Cargoes, appeared in 1896. He published over twenty collections and the play The Monkey's Paw (1907, with Louis N. Parker); he died in London on 1 September 1943.
literary_profile: Jacobs wrote the English comic short story at its most consummate: his tales of bargees, night watchmen, sailors and henpecked husbands are models of construction, with a twist at the end that is never merely mechanical, and his dialogue is the most exact rendering of London working-class speech in the period. 'The Monkey's Paw' is one of the most famous horror stories in English, and its cold economy shows the same technical mastery as the comedies.
stylistic_characteristics: The tightly constructed story with a final turn; comic dialogue in London vernacular; the domestic interior of the riverside household; the unspoken and the withheld; the horror that is implied rather than shown; a narrative voice of complete deadpan calm.
intellectual_concerns: The sea, the docks and the riverside; marriage and the henpecked husband; poverty, luck and the small windfall; superstition and the supernatural; class and the working man's world; fear and the inexplicable.
historical_significance: Jacobs is the finest English comic short-story writer of his generation and the author of one of the most famous horror stories in the language: 'The Monkey's Paw' has been adapted, anthologised and imitated for a century, and his comic stories are the technical model for the English short story from Wodehouse to Saki.

literary_identity: Poet; Poet Laureate from 1850, and the central English poet of the nineteenth century after the Romantics.
biography: Fourth son of the rector of Somersby, he was educated at Louth and Trinity College, Cambridge, where he joined the Apostles and formed the friendship with Arthur Henry Hallam that produced In Memoriam. Poems, Chiefly Lyrical (1830) and Poems (1832; dated 1833) were attacked by the Quarterly Review in 1833, and the death of Hallam in Vienna that year began the long elegy. The ten years of silence that followed ended with the two-volume Poems of 1842, which made his reputation; The Princess (1847), In Memoriam (1850) and the laureateship followed, and Maud (1855), the Idylls of the King (1859-85) and Enoch Arden (1864) made him the most widely read poet of the age. He accepted a peerage in 1884 and died at Aldworth, Surrey, on 6 October 1892; he is buried in Westminster Abbey.
literary_profile: Tennyson's art is one of exact musical notation: he is the great English poet of vowel and cadence, and the obscurity of the 1832 volume was achieved by a deliberate refinement of sound beyond sense. His subjects are loss, memory, the divided will and the natural world as a system of correspondences, and his forms range from the classical idyll and the Arthurian epic to the dramatic monologue, the dialect poem and the society ballad. In In Memoriam he invented a stanza and made it carry the largest Victorian argument about death, geology and faith.
stylistic_characteristics: Impeccable vowel music and a metrical inventiveness unmatched in English after Milton; the use of onomatopoeia and of stanzaic repetition; the framing of private grief as public statement; a pictorial and emblematic landscape; a diction that mixes the archaic and the colloquial.
intellectual_concerns: Mourning, immortality and the argument from grief; the conflict of geological time with revealed religion; the will divided between duty and desire; classical and Arthurian myth as modern moral argument; the imperial nation and its heroes; the poet's public office.
historical_significance: Tennyson set the tone of Victorian poetry and its public role; In Memoriam gave the century its language for doubt, and the Idylls its image of empire and chivalry. His influence runs through Hardy, Hopkins, Eliot and Auden, and his reinstatement after the modernist reaction has made him again the central Victorian poet.

literary_identity: Poet and dramatist; the master of the dramatic monologue and the poet who made the difficult, allusive, spoken voice the instrument of Victorian psychology.
biography: Born in Camberwell on 7 May 1812, the son of a Bank of England clerk with a large library; he was educated privately and at University College London, which he left without a degree. Pauline (1833) was published anonymously at his own expense; Paracelsus (1835) and Sordello (1840) followed, the latter's obscurity becoming a byword. Strafford was staged at Covent Garden in 1837 with Macready, and the plays of 1841-46 were collected as Bells and Pomegranates. He married Elizabeth Barrett in September 1846 and lived in Florence and Rome until her death in 1861; Men and Women appeared in 1855, Dramatis Personae in 1864, and The Ring and the Book in four volumes in 1868-69 made him famous. He returned to England in 1861 and died in Venice on 12 December 1889; he is buried in Poets' Corner.
literary_profile: Browning's central invention is the dramatic monologue as an instrument of self-betrayal: a speaker, usually at a moment of crisis, addresses an imagined listener, and the poem's meaning lies in what the speech reveals against the speaker's intention. He wrote in a deliberately rough, colloquial, parenthetical syntax and in rhymed forms whose rhymes are often grotesque, and he set the poem in the Renaissance, in the medical lecture room or in the modern drawing room indifferently. His religion of human love and of the value of the imperfect, stated most fully in the epilogue to Men and Women and in The Ring and the Book, is the intellectual centre of the work.
stylistic_characteristics: Dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice; abrupt openings; colloquial parenthesis and asyndeton; elaborate and often comic rhyme; the use of historical documents and trial records as raw material; the casuistical argument conducted in verse.
intellectual_concerns: The psychology of self-justification; the relation of art to moral action (Fra Lippo Lippi, Andrea del Sarto, A Grammarian's Funeral); religion, doubt and the value of imperfect faith (Bishop Blougram, Caliban upon Setebos); marriage and the claims of the flesh; the Renaissance as a mirror of the Victorian present; the problem of evil and the justice of God.
historical_significance: Browning made the dramatic monologue the central Victorian poetic form, and with Tennyson he dominated the poetry of the age. His influence on Pound, Eliot and the modernist long poem is direct, and The Ring and the Book is the fullest Victorian attempt to write a truth by the multiplication of partial perspectives.

literary_identity: Poet, translator and political writer; the most widely read English woman poet of the nineteenth century and the author of Sonnets from the Portuguese and Aurora Leigh.
biography: Born on 6 March 1806, the eldest of twelve children of Edward Moulton-Barrett, a Jamaican plantation owner, she was educated at home and read Greek and Hebrew as a child. A spinal illness from 1821 and the death of her brother Edward in 1840 confined her at 50 Wimpole Street, where she wrote The Seraphim (1838), Poems (1844) and the sonnets that became Sonnets from the Portuguese (1850). Her correspondence with Robert Browning began in January 1845; they married secretly in September 1846 and left for Italy, living in Pisa and Florence, where their son Pen was born in 1849. Casa Guidi Windows (1851), Aurora Leigh (1856) and Poems before Congress (1860) belong to the Italian years of the Risorgimento. She died in Florence on 29 June 1861.
literary_profile: Barrett Browning made the woman poet a public intellectual. Her subjects are the political struggles of Italy, the condition of women, slavery, child labour and the vocation of the artist, and her forms are the sonnet sequence, the verse novel, the ballad and the polemical poem. Aurora Leigh is the first English verse novel written by a woman about a woman writer, and it argues explicitly for a woman's right to an independent vocation. Her style is dense, allusive and often colloquial, and the earlier poems show the influence of Greek tragedy and of the Hebrew prophets.
stylistic_characteristics: Blank verse of sustained narrative drive; the sonnet sequence used as a single psychological document; a rhetoric of apostrophe and of political address; baroque imagery of Italy and of the Old Testament; a deliberate mixing of the domestic and the prophetic registers.
intellectual_concerns: The woman artist and the claims of vocation against marriage; Italian nationalism and the Risorgimento; slavery and the condition of the American South; child labour and social reform; religious doubt and the argument from human love; the relation of poetry to the age.
historical_significance: Barrett Browning was the most influential English woman writer of the century before George Eliot: Sonnets from the Portuguese made the amatory sonnet sequence a woman's form, and Aurora Leigh gave the nineteenth-century woman's movement its central literary text. Her Italian poems made her a figure of the Risorgimento, and her influence runs through Christina Rossetti, the Brontës and the twentieth-century feminist recovery of women's poetry.
biographical_uncertainty: The family's income derived from Jamaican sugar plantations worked by enslaved people, a fact the family concealed and which modern scholarship (and Barrett Browning's own 'The Runaway Slave at Pilgrim's Point') addresses; the marriage was kept secret from her father, who never forgave it.

literary_identity: Poet, school inspector and critic; the founder of English cultural criticism and the century's most influential theorist of the function of criticism.
biography: Born on 24 December 1822, the son of Thomas Arnold, headmaster of Rugby; he was educated at Rugby and Balliol College, Oxford, where he won the Newdigate in 1843 and was elected to a fellowship in 1845. He became private secretary to Lord Lansdowne, travelled in Europe, and was appointed an inspector of schools in 1851, a post he held for thirty-five years. In 1851 he married Frances Lucy Wightman; the death of his father in 1842 and of his son in 1868 shape the elegiac poems. The Strayed Reveller (1849), Empedocles on Etna (1852), Poems (1853) and New Poems (1867) contain the verse; from 1857 he was Professor of Poetry at Oxford, and Essays in Criticism (1865), Culture and Anarchy (1869) and Literature and Dogma (1873) made him the central Victorian critic. He died suddenly in Liverpool on 15 April 1888.
literary_profile: Arnold's criticism defines the modern idea of culture as 'the best that has been thought and said' and of criticism as 'a disinterested endeavour to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world'. His poetry is elegiac and classical, written in a restrained, slightly flat and deeply melancholic voice, and its subject is the loss of faith and the impossibility of action after the Romantics. From 1853 he deliberately suppressed Empedocles on Aetna because it dramatised a 'dialogue of the mind with itself' rather than offering a remedy, and the critical prose takes up the work the poetry could not do.
stylistic_characteristics: Classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary; elegiac stanzas and blank-verse meditation; the use of a mask or a historical figure as a screen for personal feeling; in the prose, irony, urbanity, quotation and a taste for the telling phrase ('sweetness and light', 'Philistines', 'Barbarians', 'the archery of the intellect').
intellectual_concerns: The loss of religion and the consolations of culture; the conflict of Hellenism and Hebraism; the state, the aristocracy and the middle class as objects of satire; education and the national school system; the function of criticism in a commercial age; the sea of faith and the retreat of the supernatural.
historical_significance: Arnold invented the vocabulary of English cultural criticism: 'culture', 'Philistine', 'Barbarian', 'sweetness and light', 'the best that has been thought and said' all entered the language from his prose. Culture and Anarchy is the founding text of the English critique of industrial modernity, and its argument shaped Leavis, Eliot, Raymond Williams and the whole institutional history of English studies.

literary_identity: Poet and educationalist; the most sceptical of the Victorian poets and the author of The Bothie of Tober-na-Vuolich and Amours de Voyage.
biography: Born in Liverpool on 1 January 1819, son of a cotton merchant; brought up in Charleston, South Carolina, and educated at Rugby under Thomas Arnold and at Balliol College, Oxford. He resigned his Oxford fellowship in 1848 over the Thirty-Nine Articles, was principal of University Hall, London, in 1849-52 and an examiner in the Education Office from 1852; he travelled to America and Italy in 1849 and married Blanche Smith in 1854, a cousin of Florence Nightingale, whose biography he began. He died in Florence on 13 November 1861, and his poems were collected by his wife and by his friend Matthew Arnold, whose 'Thyrsis' is his elegy.
literary_profile: Clough wrote the Victorian long poem as a debate: The Bothie, in hexameters, is a holiday romance that turns into an argument about class, education and marriage, and Amours de Voyage is an epistolary novelette in verse whose hero's paralysis of will makes him a comic and painful ancestor of the modern anti-hero. His scepticism is not agonised but dry, ironic and unresolved, and he refuses the consolations that Tennyson and Arnold supply.
stylistic_characteristics: Hexameter and loose, conversational rhymed forms; letters, journals and reported speech inside the poem; a self-mocking narrator; deliberate flatness of diction; the intrusion of contemporary politics (the Roman Republic of 1849, the Crimean War) into private love.
intellectual_concerns: Religious doubt and intellectual honesty; the relation of the educated Englishman to the working class; love and the fear of commitment; the 1848 revolutions and Italian independence; education and national life; the comic exposure of Victorian earnestness.
historical_significance: Clough is the poet in whom Victorian doubt becomes a modern, ironic intelligence rather than a crisis; his influence on Hopkins (who was his pupil at Oxford), on Arnold's elegy and on the twentieth-century long poem is out of proportion to his small output. He is now read as the missing link between the Romantic conversation poem and the modernist verse-novel.

literary_identity: Poet and Jesuit priest; the great technical innovator of Victorian poetry, whose work was almost entirely unpublished in his lifetime.
biography: Born on 28 July 1844 into a High Church family, educated at Highgate School and Balliol College, Oxford, where he was taught by Walter Pater and befriended by Robert Bridges. He became a Roman Catholic in 1866 and entered the Society of Jesus in 1868, burning his early poems; he was ordained in 1877, taught at Stonyhurst and in Lancashire, and held parish posts in London, Oxford, Glasgow and Liverpool, becoming Professor of Greek at the Royal University of Dublin in 1884. His poems were sent to Bridges and to Coventry Patmore but not published; the 'terrible' sonnets of 1885 and the Dublin poems record a crisis of desolation. He died of typhoid in Dublin on 8 June 1889, and Bridges edited the first edition in 1918.
literary_profile: Hopkins invented sprung rhythm — a metre based on stress rather than on the count of syllables, with a fixed number of stresses per line and any number of unstressed syllables between them — and inscape, the theory that every created thing has an individual pattern that the poet must perceive and render. His poetry is devotional in argument and radically modern in technique: dense alliteration, compound epithets, compressed syntax, and a rhythm that breaks the iambic habit of English verse.
stylistic_characteristics: Sprung rhythm; heavy alliteration and internal rhyme; compound and coined words ('dapple-dawn-drawn', 'selfwrung'); exclamatory syntax and abrupt ellipsis; the sonnet form used with extreme variation; a diction that draws on Anglo-Saxon and on Welsh and Latin poetry.
intellectual_concerns: The glory of God in created particularity; the Jesuit discipline and the exercises of obedience; the beauty of nature and the industrial destruction of it ('Binsey Poplars', 'God's Grandeur'); personal desolation and the dark night of the soul; death, resurrection and the 'terrible' sonnets; Wales, Lancashire and Ireland.
historical_significance: Hopkins is the technical origin of free verse's stress-based metrics in English and the ancestor of the modernist line from Pound and Eliot to the confessional poets. The posthumous 1918 edition changed the course of English poetry, and the 'terrible' sonnets are among the most powerful religious poems in the language.
biographical_uncertainty: Almost the whole corpus remained in manuscript and was published posthumously (1918, ed. Robert Bridges; the 4th edition of 1967 ed. Gardner and MacKenzie is standard). The dating of individual poems depends on autograph fair copies and on the letters to Bridges, Dixon and Patmore.
